```{r setup}
library(distributions7)
```

This vignette walks through fitting a distribution to a sample by maximum
likelihood, reading the result, checking it against the data, and simulating
from it. It assumes familiarity with distribution objects;
`vignette("defining-a-distribution")` is the place to start otherwise.

## A first fit

Every distribution has a constructor. It takes the link functions for its
parameters, but the defaults are sensible, so most of the time it is called
with no arguments:

```{r}
d <- gamma2_distrib()
d
```

We simulate some data from a known parameter value and fit the distribution back
to it. Parameters travel as a named list.

```{r}
y <- distrib_rng(d, 500, list(mu = 3, sigma2 = 2))
fit <- fit_distrib(d, y)
fit
```

The estimates recover the values from which the sample was generated, and the print
method shows them twice: on the parameter scale, and on the link
scale where the fitting actually happened. The split is explained below.

## Reading the fit

`fit_distrib()` returns an object that supports the familiar extractors:

```{r}
coef(fit)
vcov(fit)
logLik(fit)
confint(fit)
```

`coef()`, `vcov()` and `confint()` all take a `scale` argument, which returns
the same quantities on the unconstrained scale:

```{r}
coef(fit, scale = "link")
confint(fit, scale = "link")
```

The interval on the link scale is symmetric about the estimate, and the one on
the parameter scale is its image under $g^{-1}$, so the second is not
symmetric. `confint()` also takes a `level`, computed from the stored estimates
and standard errors without refitting:

```{r}
confint(fit, level = 0.99)
```

The object also carries the information criteria, the number of iterations and
the method that was actually used, and the print above shows all of them.

## Why the link scale

A gamma's mean and variance are positive; a beta's probability lives in
$(0, 1)$; a Gaussian's standard deviation is positive. Optimizing those
constrained parameters directly means fighting the boundary. Instead
`fit_distrib()` optimizes the unconstrained parameters behind each link
($\log\mu$ and $\log\sigma^2$ for the gamma), where there is no boundary to hit,
using the exact score and information that the package provides on that scale.

The estimates are then mapped back, and so are the intervals. Because a
confidence interval is built symmetrically on the link scale and pushed through
$g^{-1}$, its endpoints can never leave the parameter's domain:

```{r}
b <- bernoulli_distrib()
fit_distrib(b, rbinom(40, 1, 0.9))
```

Even with a probability estimate close to one and only forty observations, the
interval stays inside $(0, 1)$, where a symmetric interval on the probability
scale would have spilled past it.

## Choosing how it is optimized

The default is Fisher scoring, which uses the *expected* information. Two other
methods are available as optimizer objects from
[optimizers7](https://statmodels7.github.io/optimizers7/), Newton's method with
the observed Hessian and BFGS, each with the stopping rule on the gradient that
Fisher scoring uses. Fisher scoring falls back to BFGS if it fails to
converge:

```{r}
fit_newton <- fit_distrib(
  d, y, method = optimizers7::newton(criterion = optimizers7::crit_grad())
)
fit_bfgs <- fit_distrib(
  d, y, method = optimizers7::bfgs(criterion = optimizers7::crit_grad())
)

c(scoring = as.numeric(logLik(fit)),
  newton  = as.numeric(logLik(fit_newton)),
  bfgs    = as.numeric(logLik(fit_bfgs)))
```

They agree on the maximum. Fisher scoring is the default because it uses the
expected information, which stays well-behaved even where the observed Hessian
does not, and that matters for distributions with a non-smooth parameter such
as the Laplace.

The optimization runs through
[optimizers7](https://statmodels7.github.io/optimizers7/), and `method` also
accepts an optimizer object from that package, which is then used as given.
Choosing the optimizer this way also chooses its stopping rule, its line
search and its iteration budget:

```{r}
library(optimizers7)

fit_lbfgs <- fit_distrib(d, y, method = lbfgs(criterion = crit_grad(1e-12)))
fit_nm    <- fit_distrib(d, y, method = nelder_mead(maxit = 5000))

c(lbfgs = as.numeric(logLik(fit_lbfgs)),
  nelder_mead = as.numeric(logLik(fit_nm)))
c(fit_lbfgs@method, fit_nm@method)
```

Fisher scoring falls back to BFGS when it fails to converge; an optimizer
object supplied explicitly is never replaced, so the method reported is always
the method that produced the estimates.

Where the family has no closed-form expected information, Fisher scoring needs
an approximation of it. The approximation is an object passed to
`fisher_scoring()`, among `expect_opg()` (the default),
`expect_bartlett()`, `expect_integrate()` and `expect_mc(nsim = 10000)`;
`?expected_derivative_methods` compares them.

## Checking the fit against the data

A fit stores the data from which it was estimated, so it can be drawn over
them. For a
continuous distribution `plot()` shows a kernel density of the sample with the
fitted density on top:

```{r}
plot(fit)
```

For a discrete distribution it shows the observed frequencies as bars with the
fitted probability mass overlaid, because a kernel density would misrepresent
counts:

```{r}
p <- poisson_distrib()
yp <- distrib_rng(p, 300, list(mu = 4))
plot(fit_distrib(p, yp))
```

## Simulating from the fit

`simulate()` draws new samples from the fitted distribution. Each replicate has
the same length as the original data, which makes it a one-liner to build a
parametric bootstrap of any statistic:

```{r}
sims <- simulate(fit, 200, seed = 1)
dim(sims)

boot_median <- vapply(sims, median, numeric(1))
quantile(boot_median, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

It follows the convention of `stats::simulate()`: a supplied `seed` makes the draw
reproducible and is reported back on the result, and the caller's random stream
is left untouched.

## Validating a distribution numerically

Before a fit is trusted, and especially before a user-written distribution
is, `check_distrib()` runs a battery of numerical checks on it.
The checks establish that the density integrates to one, that the distribution
function agrees with the density, that the quantile inverts it, that the generator
follows it, that the analytical derivatives match finite differences on the
parameter scale, and that the score matches them on the link scale:

```{r}
invisible(check_distrib(d, list(mu = 3, sigma2 = 2)))
```

Had a mistake crept into an analytical derivative, the corresponding line would
read `FAIL`, and the size of the discrepancy is printed next to it. It is the
fastest way to catch a wrong formula.
